abstract: Dengue virus remains a major global health threat due to its four antigenically diverse serotypes and limited treatment and vaccine options. This study aimed to design and evaluate a rational tetravalent multi-epitope vaccine capable of eliciting broad cross-serotype immune responses against dengue virus. An immunoinformatics-driven strategy was employed to identify CTL, HTL, and B-cell epitopes from the NS3, NS5, and envelope domain III proteins of DENV-1 to DENV-4 based on antigenicity, allergenicity, and predicted immunogenic potential, followed by assessment of HLA population coverage. Among the selected CTL epitopes, three were completely conserved across all four serotypes, while one HTL epitope showed the highest conservation among the selected MHC class II epitopes. High-scoring linear B-cell epitopes were identified across EDIII of all four DENV serotypes, with several closely matching experimentally validated epitopes and predominantly localizing to the FG loop and DIII-DI hinge regions. The combined MHC class I and II population coverage reached 98.05% worldwide. The final vaccine construct comprised 584 amino acids incorporating 11 CTL, 14 HTL, and 7 B-cell epitopes linked to an N-terminal β-defensin adjuvant. Molecular docking, MM/GBSA calculations, and 200 ns molecular dynamics simulations demonstrated stable interactions with both TLR2 and TLR4/MD2 complexes, with docking binding energies of -16.2 and -26.0 kcal/mol and MM/GBSA binding free energies of -27.15 ± 0.54 and -52.50 ± 0.55 kcal/mol, respectively. In silico immune simulation predicted substantial lymphocyte activation, enhanced IFN-γ secretion, predicted antigen clearance, and immunoglobulin class switching. Collectively, the proposed tetravalent multi-epitope vaccine was predicted to provide broad cross-serotype epitope representation, substantial population coverage, and favorable structural and immunological profiles, supporting its potential for further vaccine development. Experimental studies in appropriate in vitro and in vivo models are warranted to further assess its immunogenicity, safety, and protective potential.
